fields: Do Not Start With This When

rows.Main Input: imaging-based ST molecule coordinates + gene identities, with optional prior segmentation or co-stain information
rows.Main Use in This Topic: cell segmentation and transcript-to-cell assignment for imaging-based spatial transcriptomics
rows.Main Output: cell segmentation boundaries plus molecule assignments
rows.Key Difference: Uses a probabilistic model of transcript composition and cell morphology and can operate from detected transcripts alone, whereas graph, deep, or nuclei-anchored alternatives rely more on learned embeddings, image features, or candidate-cell context.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 34650268 verifies the Nature Biotechnology method paper and DOI 10.1038/s41587-021-01044-w; the registry and public repository verify the primary code trace. Layer 2 synthesis: local alternatives, scale sensitivity, and boundary-risk caveat.
rows.Best First Choice When: When imaging-based ST needs a mature transcript-assignment baseline that can use transcript coordinates with or without co-stain prior information.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the primary task is raw fluorescence spot detection, image-processing support, joint image classification, or a deep transfer segmentation route.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Probabilistic transcript-based segmentation can struggle when marker density, cell overlap, or morphology priors are weak; benchmark gains are method-paper-local.

rows.Main Input: subcellular ST transcript coordinates and gene identities, with graph representations and optional pretrained transfer models
rows.Main Use in This Topic: joint noise-aware cell segmentation and molecular annotation
rows.Main Output: cell segmentation plus molecular or cell annotation outputs
rows.Key Difference: Couples segmentation with graph deep learning and transferred embeddings, adding molecular annotation and transfer-learning behavior beyond segmentation-only baselines.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 40681510 verifies the Nature Communications method paper and DOI 10.1038/s41467-025-60898-9; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: resource labels and comparison to non-annotation segmentation methods.
rows.Best First Choice When: When segmentation should be coupled to molecular annotation and transfer learning across 2D or 3D spatial transcriptomics data.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When a transparent segmentation-only route is preferred or annotation coupling could bias the downstream analysis.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Transfer learning and annotation coupling can improve robustness but may import training-set or reference-pattern bias into segmentation decisions.

rows.Main Input: high-resolution ST spots or transcripts plus imaging data
rows.Main Use in This Topic: cell segmentation and spot assignment for high-resolution spatial transcriptomics
rows.Main Output: cell assignments for high-resolution ST spots or transcripts
rows.Key Difference: Uses image-plus-sequencing information to infer spot or transcript position relative to cells, rather than relying only on transcript-coordinate composition or cell-boundary images.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 37429992 verifies the Nature Methods method paper and DOI 10.1038/s41592-023-01939-3; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: scale and closest-alternative labels.
rows.Best First Choice When: When high-resolution ST includes useful imaging data and the analysis needs spot-to-cell assignment rather than raw spot detection.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When no reliable image signal is available or the task is only fluorescence spot detection before transcript assignment.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Image-dependent assignment can inherit image-segmentation errors and may be less suitable when morphology and transcript density disagree.

rows.Main Input: imaging-based ST transcript coordinates, gene identities, and candidate cell context; optional scRNA-seq information may improve assignments
rows.Main Use in This Topic: fast transcript-to-cell link prediction for cell segmentation
rows.Main Output: transcript-to-cell links and segmented cell assignments
rows.Key Difference: Frames segmentation as heterogeneous-graph link prediction and emphasizes scalable transcript assignment, while retaining preprint evidence caveats.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 40161614 verifies the bioRxiv preprint and DOI 10.1101/2025.03.14.643160; public documentation and repository traces support code-access metadata. Layer 2 synthesis: frontier status, local alternatives, and caution around preprint benchmark claims.
rows.Best First Choice When: When large imaging-based ST transcript assignment is the focus and a graph link-prediction method with preprint-level evidence is acceptable for review.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When peer-reviewed method-paper evidence is required before selection or optional scRNA-derived priors are undesirable.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Current evidence is preprint-level; reported speed and sensitivity advantages need independent replication before being treated as general.

rows.Main Input: subcellular ST transcript data plus nuclei staining or nuclei segmentation information
rows.Main Use in This Topic: unified cell segmentation across subcellular ST platforms
rows.Main Output: cell segmentation and transcript assignment outputs
rows.Key Difference: Integrates nuclei segmentation and transcript data in a unified deep-learning framework across multiple SST platforms.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 39763408 verifies the Small Methods method paper and DOI 10.1002/smtd.202400975; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: comparison to other transcript-assignment methods and resource caveats.
rows.Best First Choice When: When subcellular ST data have nuclei information and the goal is a unified platform-spanning segmentation route.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When nuclei staining is absent, unreliable, or scientifically inappropriate as a segmentation anchor.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Nuclei-anchored segmentation may miss non-nuclear cellular extent or propagate nuclei detection errors into transcript assignment.

rows.Main Input: subcellular spatial transcriptomics data with transcript locations and morphology or cell-shape priors
rows.Main Use in This Topic: biologically informed cell segmentation for subcellular spatial transcriptomics
rows.Main Output: segmented cells and transcript-to-cell assignments for subcellular ST data
rows.Key Difference: Uses biologically informed self-supervised learning to infer cell boundaries in subcellular ST, whereas nuclei-anchored and image-plus-transcript routes rely on different priors.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 38218939 verifies the Nature Communications method paper and DOI 10.1038/s41467-023-44560-w; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: branch placement, resource cue, and local alternatives.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the task is subcellular ST cell segmentation and biologically informed self-supervised boundary inference matches the data assumptions.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the task is only histology-image support, raw spot detection, or a transparent transcript-coordinate-first baseline.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Self-supervised boundary inference may encode morphology and cell-shape assumptions; public evidence remains method-paper-local for cross-platform generalization.

rows.Main Input: Visium or related high-resolution histology or immunofluorescence images paired with spatial transcriptomics data
rows.Main Use in This Topic: image-processing and segmentation-workflow support for spatial transcriptomics histology images
rows.Main Output: processed histology or IF image features and segmentation-support outputs, not direct transcript-to-cell assignments
rows.Key Difference: Supports image processing and segmentation-oriented feature extraction for SRT workflows, rather than directly inferring cell boundaries from transcript coordinates.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 38510173 verifies the Biological Imaging method paper and DOI 10.1017/S2633903X23000235; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: support-row boundary and non-interchangeability caveat.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the missing step is high-resolution Visium histology or IF image processing that supports a segmentation workflow.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the required output is cell masks, transcript-to-cell assignments, or raw fluorescence spot coordinates.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: This is a segmentation-support boundary row; image-processing outputs should not be interpreted as direct molecular cell segmentation or transcript assignment.

rows.Main Input: high-resolution spatial transcriptomics data with cell boundary images, especially Stereo-seq-like settings
rows.Main Use in This Topic: cell-boundary based binning and generation of single-cell expression profiles from high-resolution ST
rows.Main Output: cell-boundary informed bins and single-cell gene expression profiles
rows.Key Difference: Uses cell boundary images to obtain cell-level expression profiles from high-resolution ST, making the platform and boundary-image dependence central to selection.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 38434932 verifies the GigaByte method paper and DOI 10.46471/gigabyte.110; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: platform boundary and comparison to other cell-assignment routes.
rows.Best First Choice When: When high-resolution ST already has reliable cell boundary images and the goal is cell-boundary based binning or single-cell expression profile generation.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When cell boundary images are absent, unreliable, or the task is transcript-coordinate-first segmentation without platform-specific boundary support.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Platform and boundary-image dependence can propagate image-boundary errors into cell-level expression profiles; it should not be generalized as an image-free assignment route.

rows.Main Input: 2D or 3D fluorescence microscopy images with spot-like transcript signals
rows.Main Use in This Topic: raw transcript spot detection upstream of imaging-based ST segmentation
rows.Key Difference: Detects fluorescence spots with deep stereographic flow regression; it is upstream of cell segmentation rather than a cell-boundary segmentation method.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 40481364 verifies the Nature Methods method paper and DOI 10.1038/s41592-025-02662-x; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: placement as an upstream segmentation-branch method.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the immediate problem is detecting transcript-like fluorescence spots in large noisy 2D or 3D images before cell assignment.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the requested output is segmented cells or transcript-to-cell assignments rather than spot coordinates.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Spot detection quality constrains all later transcript assignment, but high spot-level accuracy does not itself validate cell boundaries.

rows.Main Input: RNA FISH or fluorescence microscopy images with manually or synthetically annotated spot examples for training context
rows.Main Use in This Topic: automatic deep-learning spot detection for RNA FISH-derived imaging data
rows.Key Difference: Optimizes a differentiable SmoothF1 loss to directly balance false-positive and false-negative spot detection, making it a spot detector rather than a cell segmentation method.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 41265398 verifies the Cell Systems method paper and DOI 10.1016/j.cels.2025.101448; public code traces support the repository link. Layer 2 synthesis: upstream branch placement and scale caution.
rows.Best First Choice When: When RNA FISH spot detection is the primary bottleneck and automated F1-oriented spot detection is more relevant than cell-boundary segmentation.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the output must be cell masks, segmented cells, or transcript-to-cell assignments.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Optimizing spot-level F1 can still leave ambiguity for densely packed or overlapping cells; downstream segmentation needs separate validation.

rows.Main Use in This Topic: joint image-based instance segmentation and classification
rows.Main Output: segmented and classified tissue objects or cells
rows.Key Difference: Uses transformer-based multitask learning for segmentation and classification of tissue images, rather than transcript-coordinate-first cell assignment.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence: PubMed PMID 39578628 verifies the Nature Methods method paper and DOI 10.1038/s41592-024-02513-1; the public repository is recorded as an access trace. Layer 2 synthesis: boundary placement because this row is image-segmentation/classification centered rather than transcript-assignment centered.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the segmentation problem is intentionally coupled to image-based cell or tissue-object classification in multiplexed spatial-omics images.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the core input is transcript coordinates and the required output is transcript-to-cell assignment without image classification.
rows.Boundary-risk Caveat: Joint classification can improve object labeling but may entangle segmentation boundaries with class priors and image-domain bias.
